readerTitle: Two businesses went looking for customers. One knew where to look.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소·위생용품 유통업체, 소형 금속 가공 공장, 물리치료 클리닉용 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 잠재 고객은 넓게 뿌려서 찾는 것이 아니라, 가장 좋은 기존 고객에서 거꾸로 출발해 그들과 닮고 지금 필요가 생긴 곳을 찾는 것이다.
misconception: 더 많이 연락할수록 고객도 더 많이 생긴다. 명단이 클수록 좋다.

sources.text: 영업 실무의 일반 원리 (기존 우수 고객 분석, 계기가 되는 사건, 소개 영업)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 전환율 계산: 유통업체 2 ÷ 400 = 0.5%, 금속 가공 공장 5 ÷ 40 = 12.5%. 3번 카드의 '25배' 표현은 12.5 ÷ 0.5 = 25로 확인했습니다.
'소개는 비슷한 고객으로 이어지는 경우가 많다'는 일반적인 영업 관찰로만 썼고, 특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다. 수치를 추가하려면 1차 출처를 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two businesses went looking for customers. One knew where to look.
body: A cleaning-supplies distributor and a small machine shop each set out to win new business customers. Both owners gave it about the same number of hours.
The distributor contacted 400 businesses and won 2. The machine shop contacted 40 and won 5.
The difference wasn't effort or charm. It was **who they chose to contact**.

image.label: Two sellers: one with a huge pile of names, one with a short list
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽 인물은 끝없이 이어지는 전화번호 목록에 파묻혀 있고, 오른쪽 인물은 짧은 카드 몇 장을 들고 문 앞에 서 있음. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You need 10 new business customers this quarter.
body: You run a distributor of cleaning and paper supplies for local businesses. You have a few hours a week for finding new customers.
Where do you start?

options.text: Buy a list of every business in the region and call down it
options.feedback: You reach lots of people fast, but most have no need or a supplier they like. Your hours go to conversations that were never going anywhere.

options.text: Study your 10 best customers, then look for businesses just like them
options.feedback: You give up reach, but every name on your list has a real reason to buy. This is the idea in this lesson.

options.text: Run social media ads aimed at local business owners
options.feedback: Ads can bring people in without your time, but who exactly are you aiming at? Without a clear picture of your best customers, you pay to reach the wrong ones.

cards.title: Far fewer contacts, more customers.
body: The distributor bought a list of 2,000 businesses and started calling. Most had no need, or were happy with their supplier.
The machine shop first looked at its 8 best customers. Most were small farm-equipment makers that had just added a new product. It found 40 more firms like that.
Per contact, the shop did **25 times better**.

image.label: Far fewer contacts, more customers.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Finding prospects
body: A **prospect** is a person or business that has a real reason to buy from you. Not everyone who *could* buy. Someone who probably *would*.
Finding prospects means working backward from your best customers. Who are they? What was happening when they first needed you? Where can you find more people like them?
The machine shop didn't sell harder. It made a better list.

image.label: Arrows leading from a few best customers to similar businesses
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 별표가 붙은 '가장 좋은 고객' 아이콘 3개, 오른쪽에 그들과 같은 색·모양의 회사 아이콘 여러 개가 화살표로 연결됨. 다른 색·모양의 아이콘들은 흐리게 처리.

cards.title: Three questions about your best customers.
body: Pick the customers who buy often, pay on time and are easy to serve. Then ask:
list: **Who are they?** Their industry, size, location, what they make or sell
**What just changed?** A new location, a new product, a lost supplier, a new manager
**Where do they gather?** Trade groups, shared suppliers, events, even the same street
cards.callout: Then ask those customers who else they know. Good customers often know businesses like themselves.

cards.title: The distributor tries again.
body: This time the owner looks at her 10 best customers. Most are independent cafés and bakeries. And most first called her in the month they opened or expanded.
So her new list is local food businesses that are about to open or add a location. She finds them through new shop signs, local news and the equipment sellers who serve them.
35 names instead of 2,000. Fewer names, but each one has a reason to talk now.

image.label: A new bakery with a 'Coming soon' sign and a supplier at the door
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 'Coming soon' 현수막이 걸린 새 빵집 앞에서 상자를 든 유통업체 직원이 주인과 인사함. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your best customers can also narrow your view.
body: Your current customers reflect where you looked before, and some luck. With only a handful, a pattern may be chance.
Keep a small share of your time for testing a new group, or you may never find out that another market fits you better.
And a good match on paper is still only a guess. Whether a prospect is worth pursuing is the next step, not this one.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app.
body: You sell booking software to physiotherapy clinics. Your most loyal users are clinics with 3 to 6 therapists that switched from paper diaries. A colleague wants to target gyms, yoga studios and hair salons too.
Which prospect list do you build first?

options.text: Clinics with 3 to 6 therapists still booking by phone or paper, especially ones hiring
options.feedback: These look just like your best users, and hiring is a moment when booking gets messy. Smaller list, much stronger reason to talk.

options.text: Every health and wellness business in the country
options.feedback: Huge reach, but gyms and salons book in different ways. You'd spend months learning their needs instead of selling to people you already understand.

options.text: Hospital physiotherapy departments, since each deal is bigger
options.feedback: Bigger deals, but a different buyer with long approval steps. Worth testing later, not as your main list.

cards.title: Find more of your best customers, not more names.
body: Start from the customers you'd love to clone. Learn who they are, what was changing when they found you, and where their look-alikes gather.
**Try it today:** write down your three best customers. Next to each, note what was happening in their business when they first bought from you.
